descricao: Personality adjectives in opposite pairs, the grammar of character vs. temporary behavior, and the false friends that trip up Portuguese speakers.

secoes.conteudo:
Talking about people is one of the most fundamental things we do in any language. Think about the last conversation you had — how much of it was about what someone did, how they acted, or what kind of person they are? Most of it, probably.

The difference between describing someone's looks and describing their **character** is the difference between the outside and the inside. Hair and height are visible. But who someone really is — how they make you feel, what it is like to know them, whether you **trust** them — that requires a different kind of vocabulary. And that is exactly what this material is about.

You will learn the key words in pairs: each adjective alongside its natural opposite, always together. The contrast makes both words stick, and it reveals something true about how they work. Being **generous** only has meaning because **mean** exists. **Confidence** only has shape alongside **shyness**. Learning pairs gives you the full picture, not just half of it.

Before we start, one useful distinction. In English, we separate two ideas: someone's **character** and their **behavior**. Your **character** is who you are most of the time — your stable, consistent way of being in the world. Your **behavior** is how you are acting right now, in this moment. A person with a **generous** character can behave unkindly on a terrible day. Both things can be true at once. We will come back to this in the grammar section, because it changes how you use these words in a sentence.

secoes.titulo: Mood and Energy: Cheerful / Miserable, Friendly / Unfriendly
secoes.conteudo:
Let's start with the most immediately noticeable thing about a person: the energy they bring into a room.

A **cheerful** person seems happy most of the time — and their happiness spreads. They are the kind of person whose mood is contagious: you feel a little better just by being near them. The word carries a warmth that simply 'happy' does not. Its opposite is **miserable**. A **miserable** person seems deeply and persistently unhappy. They see the negative side of things before anything else. One important note: in English, **miserable** is considerably lighter than the Portuguese word 'miserável.' In English, you can be **miserable** simply because you had a terrible week. It describes a mood, not a moral condition.

**Friendly** and **unfriendly** describe how approachable someone is. A **friendly** person is warm, open, and easy to talk to — they make you feel welcome quickly, without you having to work for it. **Unfriendly** describes someone who is cold, distant, or difficult to approach. This does not make them a bad person; it simply describes the impression they give. Sometimes an **unfriendly** person is just private, or tired, or nervous around new people. The word describes the effect on you, not their intention.

secoes.titulo: How You Treat Others: Generous / Mean, Polite / Rude, Honest / Dishonest
secoes.conteudo:
This group is about the most important dimension of **character**: how someone treats the people around them.

**Generous** describes someone who gives freely — their time, their attention, their money — without calculating what they will get back. True generosity is quiet; it does not need an audience. Its opposite is **mean**. Here is something worth knowing: the word **mean** does two completely different jobs in English. As an adjective, it means unkind, stingy, or petty. As a verb, it means 'to signify.' 'What does this word **mean**?' and 'She is a **mean** person' use the same spelling but different parts of speech. You will encounter both constantly.

**Polite** describes someone with good manners — someone who says please and thank you, listens when you speak, and treats everyone — not just important people — with basic courtesy. Its opposite is **rude**. A **rude** person might interrupt you mid-sentence, forget basic courtesy, or say something that embarrasses others. Sometimes rudeness is intentional. More often it is simply thoughtlessness: not malice, just a lack of awareness of how words land on other people.

**Honest** means telling the truth even when it is uncomfortable. An **honest** person says what is real, not what you want to hear. This can sting — but it builds **trust**, and **trust** is the foundation of any real relationship. Its opposite is **dishonest** — someone who lies, hides information, or shapes the truth to serve themselves. These two only make full sense as a pair: honesty only has moral weight because dishonesty exists.

secoes.titulo: Confidence and Self-Image: Confident / Shy, Arrogant / Modest
secoes.conteudo:
These pairs describe how someone sees themselves and how comfortable they are being seen.

**Confident** describes a person who believes in themselves in a calm, steady way — not loudly, not performatively. A **confident** person speaks clearly, makes eye contact, and does not need constant reassurance. Its opposite is **shy**. A **shy** person feels nervous in social situations, especially with new people or in groups. They may go quiet, avoid eye contact, or find it hard to speak up. One important note: do not confuse **shy** with rude or cold. A **shy** person is not ignoring you — they are managing discomfort. Many shy people are warm and deeply interesting once they relax. **Shy** describes a feeling, not a fault.

**Arrogant** and **modest** are a more nuanced pair. An **arrogant** person thinks they are better than others. They dismiss people's ideas, rarely admit mistakes, and can make you feel small without even noticing. **Modest** is the opposite: someone who does not show off, even when they have every reason to. A **modest** person stays **humble** — a related word, meaning not proud — and lets their work speak for itself. The contrast with confidence is worth drawing clearly: a **confident** person believes in themselves. An **arrogant** person thinks they are better than you. Confident is admirable. Arrogant is exhausting. Very different things — and knowing the difference lets you use both words precisely.

secoes.titulo: Mind and Engagement: Curious / Incurious, Funny / Serious
secoes.conteudo:
A final group of pairs that describe how someone engages with the world and with the people in it.

**Curious** is one of the most attractive qualities in a person. A **curious** person wants to understand how things work, why things happen, and what other people think. They ask questions and actually listen to the answers. They find the world interesting — and that interest is contagious. Its opposite, **incurious**, describes someone who does not look beyond the surface and is not particularly interested in learning. In everyday English, people rarely say 'incurious' directly — they prefer 'he's not very curious' or 'she doesn't seem interested.' But knowing the concept gives you the vocabulary to think about it clearly.

**Funny** and **serious** sit at opposite ends of another important scale. Someone **funny** makes you laugh naturally and without effort. The best funny people are not performing — they are just themselves, and somehow that is consistently entertaining. **Serious** describes someone who is focused, earnest, and not particularly playful. This is not a criticism: **serious** people think carefully and follow through. As **personality** traits, **funny** and **serious** pull in opposite directions, and knowing both gives you the full range of descriptions you will need.

secoes.titulo: Grammar: 'Is' vs. 'Is Being' — This Will Surprise You
secoes.conteudo:
This section surprises most people who have been studying English for years. Once you understand it, something shifts — your English suddenly sounds much more natural.

You already know 'She is funny.' Simple present. This sentence means that being **funny** is part of her **character** — who she is most of the time. She was **funny** yesterday, she will be **funny** tomorrow. That is just who she is.

But what if she is normally very **serious** — and today, in this conversation, she is making jokes and being playful? In English, you say something different. You say: 'She is being funny.' Same adjective. Different structure. Different meaning entirely.

The structure is: am / is / are + being + adjective. This is the present continuous of the verb 'to be.' It signals one very specific thing: this is how someone is acting right now, in this moment — not who they are as a general rule. 'Why is he being so rude?' — He is not normally a **rude** person, but right now his **behavior** is **rude** and you are surprised. 'Stop being boring!' — You are asking someone to change how they are acting in this specific conversation. 'She is being really generous today' — She is acting **generously** right now; maybe this is unusual for her.

Now compare: 'John is arrogant' — that is his permanent **personality**, always. 'John is being arrogant' — he is acting **arrogantly** right now, but maybe he is not always like this; maybe he is nervous, or tired, or out of character today. One structure for **character**. One for **behavior**. The contrast was always there — now you can express it.

One rule: this only works with adjectives that describe **behavior** — things a person can choose to do. You cannot say 'She is being tall' because height is not a choice. But you can say 'She is being shy' because in that moment, shyness is something she is actively doing.

Three traps come up constantly when describing **character**, and all three involve words that look familiar to Portuguese speakers.

**Sensible** and **sensitive**. These look nearly identical and mean almost opposite things. **Sensible** means practical and reasonable — someone who makes good decisions and thinks before acting. 'Be sensible!' means: use your head, do the smart thing. **Sensitive** means someone who feels things deeply — easily affected, easy to hurt, emotionally reactive. A **sensitive** person cries at sad films; a **sensible** person solves the problem. In Portuguese, 'sensível' maps to **sensitive**, not **sensible**. If you say 'I'm very sensible' in English, people will think you are calm and rational — not emotional.

**Sympathetic**. In Portuguese, 'simpático' means **friendly**, warm, and easy to like. In English, **sympathetic** means something quite different: you understand and share someone's pain or difficulty — you feel it with them. It is about empathy during hard times. 'She was very sympathetic' means she was emotionally present and caring when someone was suffering — not that she is fun to be around. For that idea, use **friendly**, **warm**, or **nice**.

**Miserable**. In Portuguese, 'miserável' is a strong word — it suggests poverty, wretchedness, moral failure. In English, **miserable** simply means very unhappy. 'I'm miserable today' just means today is going very badly. The word is considerably lighter and more everyday in English. It describes a mood — nothing more.
